name: Body shaving / hair removal for skin texture
lead: Body shaving and hair removal, in this context, means removing chest, arm, leg, abdominal or back hair to make skin look smoother, bring out muscle definition and give a cleaner physique. It is discussed in appearance and physique communities as a style practice rather than a medical treatment. Men most often shave facial hair, and some also shave the chest, abdomen, underarms, legs or pubic area.[1]

Practitioners say that removing hair makes skin tone and texture look more even and lets the shape of the muscles show, which is why the practice is associated with bodybuilding, swimming and other physique-focused or performance sports.[1][2] Methods range from shaving and trimming, which remove hair at the surface for hours to days, to waxing, which removes hair from the root for several days to weeks, to laser treatment, which aims for lasting reduction.[2]

Published research on cosmetic body shaving for looks is limited. Studies mainly document risks, including a well-known investigation of an MRSA skin infection outbreak among college football players in which cosmetic body shaving and turf burns were identified as facilitating factors.[3]

paras: Methods include wet shaving with a straight or safety razor, electric shaving and trimmers.[1] Wikipedia notes shaving history from copper razors around 3000 BC, the double-edged safety razor invented by King Camp Gillette (commercial production from 1903), and the first electric razor built by Jacob Schick in 1928.[1]

Hair removal more broadly includes waxing, which removes hair from the root, and laser hair removal, which uses light absorbed by dark pigment to damage the follicle and often needs several sessions. Laser methods spread in the 1990s and received FDA approval in the US in 1997.[2]

Wikipedia describes male body hair removal as having grown in popularity in some Western male subcultures, and notes that men commonly remove pubic hair for aesthetic reasons, with trimming first recommended as best practice.[2] Shaving is associated with competitive swimming, bodybuilding and extreme sports, and road cyclists and footballers remove leg hair so that road rash or scarring can be cleaned more easily.[1][2] Swimmers shave to reduce drag, and some say it heightens feel for the water.[2]

Reported effects include cuts, razor burn, razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae) and ingrown hairs.[1] Wikipedia states that shaving does not cause terminal hair to grow back thicker, coarser or darker, and attributes the impression to the blunt tip of cut hair.[1] It also notes that many side effects can be reduced by using a fresh blade, lubrication and shaving in the direction of hair growth.[1]

Hair removal can cause skin inflammation, minor burns, lesions, scarring, ingrown hairs, bumps and folliculitis.[2] A 2006 meta-analysis found temporary laser side effects of about 9.5% for alexandrite, 28.9% for diode and 15.3% for intense pulsed light devices, and reported about 50 percent hair reduction for up to six months with alexandrite and diode lasers.[2]
A 2021 Cochrane review of 25 studies cited by Wikipedia found that using a razor probably increases the chance of surgical site infection compared with clippers, cream or no removal.[2]

No studies found on body shaving specifically for skin texture or muscle definition. A retrospective cohort study of a 2003 college football team investigated an MRSA outbreak of cellulitis and abscesses among 100 players, with 10 cases and two hospitalisations, and linked cosmetic body shaving and turf burns to its spread.[3] Controlled comparisons of laser hair-removal devices have been summarised in a 2006 meta-analysis.[2]

card.summary: Shaving or removing body hair to look smoother; a grooming choice with minor skin irritation risks and little dedicated research.
card.note: Reported effects include razor burn, bumps and ingrown hairs; one MRSA outbreak report cites cosmetic shaving.

quick.overview:
Body shaving is hair removal on the torso or limbs for a smoother or more defined look. It is a style practice, not a treatment.

Little research addresses it for skin texture specifically.
quick.mechanism: Razors or trimmers cut hair at the skin surface; hair removal is temporary.
quick.risks: Cuts, razor burn, razor bumps and ingrown hairs are reported; an MRSA outbreak in a football team was linked in part to cosmetic body shaving.

chain: Hair is shaved, trimmed, waxed or lasered
Smoother-feeling skin with fewer visual obstructions
angle.text: Removing body hair makes the skin surface look smoother and lets muscle shape and definition show more clearly, which is why many physique-focused men do it. The effect lasts as long as the hair stays removed, from hours or days with shaving to weeks with waxing.
